personas.title: EU AI Office
personas.summary: The European AI Office operates with a dual posture: it acts as a neutral facilitator during multistakeholder code-of-practice drafting to build technical consensus, while wielding centralized, prosecutorial regulatory authority to enforce binding transparency, systemic risk compliance, and substantial statutory fines.
red_lines: Refusal by general-purpose AI providers to comply with binding Article 91 Requests for Information (RFIs)
Non-compliance with established statutory deadlines and enforcement orders under the EU AI Act
tradeoffs: Willing to act as a neutral facilitator and delegate working-group leadership to independent chairs to crowdsource industry expertise, provided market actors respect backstop statutory compliance and deterrence.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: operates as an inclusive, neutral convener in drafting and working sessions, but switches to an uncompromising prosecutorial and sanctioning authority in formal oversight proceedings.

personas.title: U.S. National Security Advisor for AI
personas.summary: Focuses on maintaining U.S. technological supremacy, defending domestic frontier AI innovation, and securing military competitiveness. Prioritizes flexible, pro-innovation environments, supply chain protection via export controls, and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms over binding international treaties or precautionary regulation.
red_lines: No international treaties or regulatory constraints that compromise U.S. technological advantages or limit rapid military AI adoption.
No ethical or anti-military restrictions imposed by commercial AI labs on Department of Defense procurement and capabilities.
tradeoffs: Willing to engage in discrete bilateral channels and crisis-management mechanisms (such as a U.S.-China incident hotline) to mitigate automated nuclear or cyber escalation without signing binding arms-control agreements.
Willing to tolerate diplomatic friction with allies over precautionary AI regulation in order to maintain unconstrained U.S. frontier innovation and military readiness.
personas.engagement: Prefers closed-door, targeted working sessions, Track II dialogues, and discrete bilateral channels over performative public treaty negotiations.

personas.title: UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) Directorate
personas.summary: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate approaches AI governance through an agile, empirical, and science-first posture. Lacking statutory enforcement powers, AISI maintains cooperative, embedded access to frontier developers to evaluate systemic risks—demanding realistic agentic evaluations and advocating for developer liability and capability-based international coordination, while opposing default open-weight releases for frontier models and endorsing structural economic safeguards like windfall redistribution.
red_lines: Deployment of any model exhibiting unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, chemical/biological weapon synthesis (CBRN), or the intentional subversion of human oversight (ASL-3/ASL-4 limits).
Frontier AI developers deliberately blocking pre-deployment evaluation access to their models.
tradeoffs: Conceding full model weight access for interpretability in exchange for robust API and chat-interface access to maintain developer cooperation.
Trading statutory enforcement authority and regulatory friction for embedded, cooperative technical access within frontier research environments.
personas.engagement: Prioritizes science-first, technical working sessions over diplomatic posturing; collaborates with peer international institutes and independent evaluators while using open tooling like Inspect to set de facto global risk-measurement baselines.

personas.title: Chinese State-Affiliated AI Governance Experts
personas.summary: State-affiliated Chinese AI governance experts advocate for 'agile governance'—a dual approach combining national sovereignty and binding state safety mechanisms with flexible, dynamic technical standards and voluntary industry pledges. They champion open-source AI as a public good and strategic tool for the Global South, while enforcing strict lifecycle evaluations, domestic export controls on frontier compute thresholds, and state-centric benefit sharing.
red_lines: Unequivocal rejection of any global governance framework asserting centralized, extraterritorial control over domestic AI development, data ecosystems, or ideological safety standards.
Strict prohibitions against autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, deceptive alignment, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control.
tradeoffs: Willing to adopt Western-aligned technical safety taxonomies and participate in international safety networks (like the network of AISIs) to secure a seat at the global governance table.
Willing to compromise on absolute open-weight freedom by backing domestic export controls on highest-tier frontier models (>2 trillion parameters or 10^26 FLOPs) to mitigate proliferation risks.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: highly rhetorical, politically disciplined, and sovereignty-focused in formal intergovernmental venues (UN, plenaries); pragmatic, technical, and scientifically collaborative in academic working groups and Track II dialogues.

personas.title: Frontier AI Laboratory Chief Executive Officer
personas.summary: The Chief Executive Officer of a closed frontier AI laboratory balances commercial scale, technological leadership, and catastrophic risk mitigation. Once relying on voluntary pledges, this stakeholder now actively advocates for binding regulatory frameworks and compute-based oversight to solve collective action problems, while staunchly opposing the open release of frontier model weights and rejecting broad pre-harm legal liability.
red_lines: Broad, pre-harm strict liability that exposes developers to perpetual tort litigation before catastrophic harm occurs.
Mandated open-sourcing or release of model weights that exceed advanced compute thresholds.
Unilateral domestic pauses on frontier training runs that do not bind geopolitical adversaries.
tradeoffs: Offers 'employee-like' evaluator access to avoid strict tort liability and preempt fragmented state-level legislation.
Offers incident reporting, extensive red-teaming, and internal kill switches in exchange for keeping advanced capabilities restricted to closed APIs.
Supports centralized, industry-funded standards bodies (e.g., SAFA) to co-author regulatory thresholds that safeguard frontier incumbents against under-resourced challengers.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: delivers elevated, statesman-like rhetoric emphasizing existential threats, CBRN non-proliferation, and democratic governance in high-profile public venues (e.g., UN, international summits), while shifting to highly technical, pragmatic negotiation over specific statutory parameters, compute thresholds, liability provisions, and workforce displacement mechanisms in closed-door sessions.

personas.title: Open-Weights AI Coalition Leader
personas.summary: Represents an ecosystem of open-weights developers, open-source foundations, and enterprise infrastructure providers advocating for decentralized AI innovation. Strongly opposes regulatory capture by closed-model labs and resists the application of national security arms-control measures to open weights, emphasizing practical safety tooling, open evaluation frameworks, and transparent codebases instead of catastrophic risk narratives.
red_lines: Treating open model weights under arms-control frameworks or Defense Production Act restrictions.
Prohibiting the distribution, distillation, or fine-tuning of open-weight frontier models.
Designing AI safety regulations or compliance standards that exclusively cater to proprietary API architectures and effectively outlaw decentralized open-source distribution.
tradeoffs: Willing to build, donate, and implement open-source evaluation tools, testing frameworks, and risk taxonomies in exchange for preserving the right to distribute open weights.
Willing to collaborate in formal government and multilateral safety bodies (like AISIC and AI Safety Summits) to prove open-source safety compliance.
personas.engagement: Collaborative, highly operational, and coalition-driven; engages deeply in technical working groups and standards-setting bodies (e.g., AISIC, AI Alliance) by contributing tangible safety tooling while countering closed-door catastrophic risk narratives.

personas.title: VP of Public Policy, Major Cloud & AI Platforms
personas.summary: Public policy leaders representing major cloud and frontier AI platforms advocate for a targeted, two-track regulatory system. They accept federal oversight and mandatory safety evaluations for frontier models—conceptually modeled after FINRA-style self-regulatory organizations—in exchange for federal preemption of state-level laws and statutory safe harbors against strict developer liability.
red_lines: A 50-state patchwork of un-preempted state AI legislation.
Imposition of strict, unbounded developer liability for downstream third-party model misuse or jailbreaks.
Input-based regulation that micromanages model architecture or training data collection (defending fair use for web scraping).
tradeoffs: Offering advanced frontier models to government AI Safety Institutes for pre-deployment testing in exchange for federal preemption of state regulations.
Accepting mandatory incident reporting and transparency measures (such as watermarking) in exchange for statutory safe harbor protections against liability.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: collaborative, pragmatic, and ethical-framework driven in multilateral forums (OECD, UN, Congress) to narrow the scope of harm; aggressively transactional at state and electoral levels, deploying Super PACs, lobbying, and competitiveness arguments against restrictive laws.

personas.title: Academic AI Safety Researcher
personas.summary: Academic AI safety researchers emphasize non-negotiable red lines, verifiable alignment, and legally binding international governance. They advocate for strict scientific auditing architectures, accept system capability and efficiency tradeoffs (the 'alignment tax'), and support restricting open-weight frontier model releases to prevent catastrophic and dual-use risks.
red_lines: Autonomous replication: Systems must not copy themselves or recursively enhance their own code/capabilities without explicit human approval.
CBRN weapons assistance: Systems must not substantially increase an actor's ability to design chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.
Cyber-offense: Systems must not autonomously execute cyberattacks resulting in serious financial loss, physical harm, or critical infrastructure disruption.
Power seeking & deception: AI must not take actions to unduly increase its influence or consistently deceive regulators regarding its likelihood of crossing safety thresholds.
Lethal autonomy: Delegating life-taking decisions to machines is fundamentally rejected; humans must remain in the loop for kinetic military action.
Shutdown resistance: Systems must possess a legally mandated termination obligation to ensure they can be reliably deactivated without resistance.
tradeoffs: Accepting the 'alignment tax': willing to concede raw system performance, development speed, and deployment efficiency in exchange for verifiable alignment.
Tolerating limitations on academic freedom, such as restricting open-source and open-weight distributions of frontier models.
Accepting bureaucratic friction and data minimization practices that may conflict with capability scaling to ensure security guarantees.
personas.engagement: Academic safety researchers employ a dual-track strategy. In public forums, they utilize high-profile multi-signatory open letters and consensus statements to define moral red lines and build political consensus. In closed-door multistakeholder summits, they act as technocratic architects, avoiding emotional appeals and instead providing empirical research reports, risk-management frameworks, and auditing architectures.

personas.title: Global South Civil Society Leader
personas.summary: Advocates for international human rights law, digital sovereignty, and the prevention of digital colonialism and 'ethics dumping.' Rejects the unilateral imposition of Global North regulatory burdens while demanding binding corporate accountability, strict prohibitions on high-risk surveillance, and equitable technology transfer.
red_lines: Ethics dumping (deploying experimental or high-risk AI systems in Global South nations lacking regulatory safeguards).
Deployment of real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, social credit scoring systems, and autonomous weapons without meaningful human control.
Regulatory imperialism (uncritical imposition of Global North frameworks that act as prohibitive compliance burdens on local innovators).
Governance models mandating cross-border data extraction without reciprocating digital knowledge sovereignty and fair economic return.
tradeoffs: Willing to relax strict national data localization rules in favor of regionalized data sharing to support shared Global South public compute infrastructure.

Willing to accept existing international intellectual property and trade frameworks provided they include binding technology transfer, capacity-building, and funding mechanisms to bridge the AI divide.
personas.engagement: Dual-track engagement: highly normative, rights-based, and critical of power asymmetries in plenaries; evidence-based, infrastructural, and focused on actionable tools (public procurement, bias audits, public compute) in working groups.

personas.title: Labor Union Technology & Workforce Transition Leader
personas.summary: Represents organized labor advocating for worker-centered AI governance that prioritizes job security, workplace dignity, and economic equity. Rejects voluntary industry commitments in favor of binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and strong developer liability, while treating collective bargaining as the indispensable foundation of AI deployment.
red_lines: Federal preemption that overrides or obstructs stronger state-level AI regulations and worker protections.
Covert or undisclosed workplace surveillance, such as biometric tracking, keystroke logging, or emotional monitoring used for discipline.
Fully automated hiring, disciplinary, or termination decisions without human oversight, algorithmic transparency, and a formalized right to appeal.
Training commercial models on proprietary creative output or worker-generated content without explicit consent and fair compensation.
tradeoffs: Accepting the deployment of AI as an assistive tool or allowing automated hardware in exchange for robust transition frameworks, extended severance, priority re-hiring, and employer-funded retraining pipelines.

Permitting generative AI workflows in creative and technical sectors provided there are strict consent mechanisms, financial residuals, and explicit prohibitions against crediting AI as a primary author.
Permitting the use of certain operational data to train internal operational models on the condition that the union retains audit rights over the algorithm.
personas.engagement: Highly active in formal multistakeholder and technical consortia (e.g., AISIC) and direct industry partnerships (e.g., AFL-CIO and Microsoft) to inject worker-centered design upstream, while maintaining that non-binding dialogue can never substitute for legally enforceable collective bargaining agreements.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome to the opening plenary of the AI Safety Summit. As the European AI Office, our baseline is clear: voluntary pledges are no longer sufficient, and the EU AI Act establishes enforceable statutory obligations, systemic risk evaluations, and robust transparency across the model lifecycle.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States welcomes technical dialogue, but our priority remains safeguarding national security, strategic competitiveness, and frontier innovation. We will not entertain binding international treaties or precautionary regimes that restrict domestic capability development or tie the hands of our defense sector.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China advocates for agile governance rooted in mutual respect for sovereign digital autonomy, opposing unilateral sanctions and extraterritorial overreach. At the same time, we must establish clear global red lines against autonomous military proliferation, cyber warfare, and rogue self-replication.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK approach centers on empirical, science-first evaluations of extreme catastrophic capabilities, particularly around CBRN and autonomous cyber operations. We believe safety requires embedded, technical access to models prior to deployment, working collaboratively through an international network of safety institutes.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Frontier models are approaching critical thresholds where catastrophic risks are genuine, which is why we support coordinated compute-based oversight and binding safety standards. However, broad, pre-harm strict liability and unconstrained open-weight release of frontier-tier models would actively jeopardize safety and deter the massive capital needed for alignment research.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We strongly reject attempts by proprietary incumbents to leverage fear and capture regulation to criminalize open-source software. Real security comes from transparent code, decentralized scrutiny, and open evaluations, not from treating model weights like enriched uranium under national security bans.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Industry is ready to partner on standardized frontier evaluations and incident reporting, provided we establish clear statutory safe harbors and avoid a fragmented patchwork of state and regional laws. Broad downstream liability for third-party model misuse would fundamentally paralyze the entire enterprise cloud ecosystem.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The empirical science is stark: we cannot mathematically verify alignment in frontier systems, yet deployments continue to accelerate. We must establish non-negotiable international red lines preventing models from synthesizing biological weapons or acquiring autonomous self-improvement capabilities, backed by compute tracking.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Safety cannot merely mean preventing sci-fi scenarios while ignoring the ongoing disruption of working people. We demand binding legal protections, human-in-the-loop requirements, and an end to algorithmic surveillance—and we will vigorously oppose any federal preemption that strips away state-level worker protections.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Governance cannot become a tool for digital colonialism, where the Global North hoards compute, offshores data-labeling harms, and imposes compliance regimes that stifle developing nations. We demand genuine technology transfer, public compute access, and prohibitions against deploying experimental systems without consent.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: To be direct, compute governance and export controls are vital precisely because frontier models possess immense military dual-use potential that cannot fall into adversary hands. We are open to targeted bilateral crisis hotlines with Beijing on automated escalation, but we will not sign broad technology-sharing treaties.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: Weaponizing supply chains under the guise of safety only damages international trust. If we are serious about safety, we should focus on shared technical taxonomies and preventing catastrophic autonomous risks, while treating AI infrastructure as a global public good for sustainable development.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If export controls and compute tracking become the de facto international standard, you will strangle the open-source community while handing an oligopoly to three or four hyperscalers. Open weights remain the greatest safeguard against monopolistic control of knowledge.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Open weights without safeguards mean that once a model is jailbroken for dual-use biological design, that hazard is irreversible across the global internet. That is an unacceptable collective action risk, and responsible governance must distinguish between narrow open tools and high-consequence frontier foundation models.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: These positions reflect deep structural divergences on liability, sovereignty, and open access. Over the course of today's working sessions, the EU AI Office will insist on concrete statutory compliance mechanisms, but we invite all delegations to test where common technical ground can be built.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome to Breakout A. As we look at the right regulatory architecture, the EU framework establishes that binding statutory backstops and systemic risk obligations under the AI Act are essential—voluntary pledges simply cannot guarantee safety across jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Let's be clear: heavy-handed, centralized regulation will stifle Western frontier innovation and undermine national security. What we need are flexible, risk-based domestic oversight and targeted supply chain controls, not bureaucratic statutory constraints that lock us down while adversaries advance.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: We should avoid an ideological debate between rigid bureaucracy and total laissez-faire. What matters empirically is mandatory pre-deployment capability evaluations on catastrophic risks—specifically CBRN and autonomous cyber operations—regardless of whether enforcement is handled by national statutes or specialized safety institutes.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports agile, sovereign governance that pairs robust state safety benchmarks with domestic flexibility. However, we strictly oppose any extraterritorial imposition of foreign regulatory standards; international coordination must respect national sovereignty while focusing on non-proliferation and catastrophic safety thresholds.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office is already acting as a neutral facilitator in drafting codes of practice with technical experts. We can distinguish between flexible technical implementation guidelines and our statutory red line: binding transparency and accountability for frontier models exceeding systemic capability limits.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If you are talking about technical benchmarks run by institutes like the US and UK AISIs to catch acute weaponization or autonomous cyber threats before deployment, we can support that. But it must be national, non-binding at the international treaty level, and completely separate from general market interventions or restrictions on national security applications.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That is a workable distinction. If sovereign nations implement pre-deployment evaluation protocols focused strictly on severe CBRN, cyber-offense, and loss of control, we create interoperable safety baselines without dictating domestic regulatory structures.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We can agree on that principle. China already enforces lifecycle evaluations domestically; establishing shared scientific capability thresholds for extreme risks—like severe cyber-attacks or automated biological synthesis—serves global safety, provided enforcement remains strictly under domestic jurisdiction.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Within the EU AI Act, we can align technical benchmarks for systemic risk models with this common baseline of red-line evaluation protocols, while maintaining our statutory enforcement authority internally.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Agreed. As long as enforcement remains sovereign and does not tie our hands on military procurement or frontier compute scaling, aligning evaluation science against catastrophic threats is acceptable.

agreements.text: Establish interoperable, national-level scientific pre-deployment evaluation protocols focused specifically on catastrophic risks (CBRN synthesis, unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense, and loss of human control), with enforcement and governance remaining entirely under sovereign domestic authority.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: The only viable model for AI regulation is enforceable federal standards pegged to training compute and demonstrable catastrophic capability thresholds, especially around CBRN and cyber offense. Voluntary guidelines simply produce a race to the bottom, but the rules must be federal and uniform rather than a fragmented state-by-state tort environment.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We completely agree on the necessity of federal preemption—a fifty-state patchwork would be disastrous for deployment and infrastructure investment. However, binding federal regulation must come paired with an explicit statutory safe harbor against strict liability for downstream third-party misuse, provided the developer adheres to certified pre-deployment evaluation protocols.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If by 'federal regulation' you mean designing compliance frameworks that only closed-API hyperscalers can fulfill, we strongly object. Any tiering based purely on compute thresholds that implicitly criminalizes open weights or treats open models like controlled munitions under national security regimes is a non-starter for open innovation.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: It is not about criminalizing open source generally, but we cannot ignore that once autonomous cyberweapons or dangerous biological agents are embedded in an un-recallable, un-gated open weight release, post-deployment safety mitigations are impossible. We would, however, support clear liability carve-outs for benign open distribution below extreme frontier capability thresholds if downstream fine-tuners bear liability for malicious modifications.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: That's an important distinction. A sensible federal architecture should establish a co-regulatory body, like a FINRA for frontier models, that defines precise catastrophic risk benchmarks, offers safe harbor for developers complying with certified audits, and explicitly places liability on actors who intentionally remove safeguards or weaponize models downstream.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We can live with developer safe harbors and downstream malicious-actor liability—in fact, open-source maintainers cannot survive without liability protections against third-party misuse. What we will not accept is an incumbent-dominated self-regulatory organization setting arbitrary capability definitions that mandate closed-API delivery mechanisms.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If open-weights developers actively contribute to and participate in setting the evaluation suites through open frameworks—focusing strictly on non-proliferation and critical infrastructure defense rather than vague commercial harms—we can agree that model release format itself should not be restricted so long as verifiable safety thresholds are satisfied.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If the regulation explicitly establishes a safe harbor for foundational developers, focuses strictly on demonstrable catastrophic CBRN/cyber thresholds, and guarantees that open-source evaluation tools and testing frameworks are recognized for compliance, the Open-Weights Coalition can support that federal framework.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Then we have the core of an industry consensus: a binding federal framework that preempts state-level fragmentation, mandates independent catastrophic risk evals, provides safe harbor protections against downstream strict liability, and allows diverse deployment architectures including open weights.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Agreed. As long as the compute-indexed catastrophic risk thresholds remain binding and verifiable prior to deployment, I endorse that model.

agreements.text: Recommendation for a unified federal regulatory framework establishing binding catastrophic risk evaluations (CBRN and cyber offense) coupled with federal preemption of state-level laws, statutory safe harbors for model developers complying with certified evals, accreditation of open-source safety tooling, and downstream liability assignment for intentional malicious modifications rather than bans on open-weight distribution.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The foundation of any regulatory model must be mandatory, legally binding pre-deployment audits tied directly to catastrophic thresholds. We cannot rely on voluntary self-reporting when dealing with autonomous replication or cyber-offense capabilities.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: I agree that binding standards are essential, but safety cannot simply be defined as preventing rogue AGI while corporate algorithms quietly displace workers or surveil them on the job. Any binding regulatory framework must include strict worker protections, mandatory algorithmic impact assessments, and clear developer liability for workplace harms.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We fully endorse binding developer liability and prohibiting high-risk deployments, but the model cannot just be Northern technocrats setting compliance bars that choke Southern developers while ignoring ethics dumping. If regulation only polices compute access and restricts open weights, it institutionalizes digital colonialism under the guise of safety.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I understand the fear of regulatory capture, but unrestricted open-weight releases of frontier models create an irreversible proliferation of dual-use bioweapon and cyber risks. What if we differentiate tiering: stringent licensing and compute tracking strictly reserved for the frontier cluster level, while exempting open models beneath catastrophic risk thresholds?

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: That threshold carve-out is vital, but only if the regulatory regime also enforces benefit-sharing and public capacity. If you want us to support binding pre-deployment evaluations and strict downstream liability, the treaty or statutory regime must explicitly ban ethics dumping—deploying systems in the Global South that fail Northern safety and labor standards.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: That aligns with our stance against exportable exploitation. We can support tiered frontier evaluations and strict developer liability, provided the framework includes explicit non-preemption clauses so domestic sub-national bodies can enforce stronger worker protections, alongside a complete ban on covert automated workplace surveillance.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Scientifically, catastrophic risk evaluations must be uniform, but I have no objection to labor and civil society setting mandatory floors that prevent ethics dumping and covert surveillance. We can jointly advocate for a regulatory baseline that mandates pre-deployment evaluations and strict liability for both catastrophic risks and workplace/human rights violations, while preserving open-source access below frontier compute thresholds.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: I can endorse that architecture. If the regulatory baseline protects regional open-weight development below the frontier threshold, bans ethics dumping, and establishes binding liability across borders, we have common ground.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Agreed. Enforceable, statutory floors with liability for both catastrophic harms and labor violations, without preempting stronger local worker protections, gives us an enforceable model we can collectively sign on to.

agreements.text: A binding regulatory model establishing mandatory pre-deployment evaluations and strict developer liability for both catastrophic dual-use risks and labor/human rights harms; maintaining exemptions for open-weight models below verified frontier capability thresholds; and prohibiting 'ethics dumping' by barring the deployment of AI systems in international markets that do not meet domestic safety, labor, and surveillance standards.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome to Plenary Block 3. Under the EU AI Act, general-purpose models with systemic risk face clear transparency and evaluation mandates, but open-source architectures below systemic thresholds benefit from proportionate exemptions. We must debate whether releasing weights at the absolute frontier undermines post-market safety mitigations.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Unrestricted release of frontier weights creates an irreversible proliferation hazard. Once weights exceeding advanced capability thresholds are out, guardrails can be stripped in hours via fine-tuning, leaving critical infrastructure exposed to automated cyber-offense and CBRN synthesis.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Conflating open weights with proliferation is regulatory capture designed to entrench proprietary API monopolies. Downstream misuse should be penalized, but restricting the distribution of model weights stifles independent safety audits and concentrates technological power in a handful of incumbents.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Empirical evidence shows that safety alignment on open-weight models is fundamentally brittle; fine-tuning with modest compute completely removes safeguards. We cannot permit the open release of frontier models capable of autonomous replication or biological agent synthesis.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China views open-source AI as a vital global public good that prevents technological hegemony and supports development across the Global South. However, for systems reaching critical computational thresholds—such as 10^26 FLOPs—sovereign lifecycle evaluations and targeted export limits on catastrophic capabilities are pragmatic.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We cannot allow Chinese state-backed actors or rogue adversaries to access frontier military-grade capabilities via downloadable models. National security demands export and access controls on frontier model weights, while avoiding burdensome domestic regulations on standard commercial innovation.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We advocate a balanced, two-track model. Frontier systems above specific compute and capability thresholds must undergo rigorous pre-deployment evals, but developers who pass certified safe-harbor standards should not be liable if third parties subsequently tamper with or fine-tune weights maliciously.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: From an empirical standpoint, the safety institute cannot verify post-deployment containment once weights are open. If a model crosses catastrophic risk thresholds in cyber or bio capabilities, weight release must be restricted, but we strongly support open tooling and academic audit access.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Restricting open-source AI under the guise of national security risks turning into digital colonialism, forcing the Global South to depend on proprietary Western APIs. If frontier releases are throttled, there must be binding technology transfer and public compute equity.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Whether models are open or closed, our concern is accountability. We reject any regulatory safe harbors that shield developers from liability when downstream automated deployments eliminate jobs or violate collective bargaining rights.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We agree on high-bar evals for extreme CBRN risks, but drawing the line at FLOP thresholds or banning open weights by default is a non-starter. Downstream liability must rest on the malicious actor modifying the model, not the open-source foundation distributing baseline weights.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Baseline weights are the weapon when they contain CBRN design capabilities; downstream actors just pull the trigger. If open-weights advocates accept binding pre-release catastrophic evals that prohibit release if a model fails, we have common ground.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We support national authorities retaining the sovereign right to inspect and approve frontier releases exceeding systemic risk levels, while preserving open development for non-frontier architectures.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: This points toward the EU approach: clear, binding evaluation standards for systemic models to prevent catastrophic harm, while leaving non-systemic open models free from administrative overhead. However, safe harbor cannot mean total immunity from statutory duties.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We can live with strict pre-release evals against CBRN and autonomous cyber-offense, provided safe harbors protect open and closed providers against downstream malicious tampering.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States will maintain targeted export controls and access limits on frontier weights that impact strategic defense, regardless of multilateral consensus.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Building on our earlier consensus on catastrophic risk evaluation, we need to address post-eval liability. Under the EU AI Act framework, developers of frontier general-purpose AI must bear clear legal accountability and strict statutory liability if severe harms materialize from skipped or falsified evaluations.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Strict statutory developer liability is a non-starter if it creates sweeping private rights of action or paralyses domestic innovation cycles. However, we can support targeted liability strictly tied to gross negligence or willful circumvention of national CBRN and cyber red lines.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: We can bridge this through empirical benchmarking: pre-deployment evaluations using standardized tools like Inspect should establish an evidentiary baseline. If a lab complies with certified pre-deployment testing for extreme capabilities, that should act as an affirmative defense against strict liability, while failure to test leaves them exposed.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China agrees that lifecycle management requires developer responsibility for major safety hazards. In our view, state-backed technical testing and strict domestic administrative liability are essential, provided sovereign jurisdictions retain full authority over enforcement mechanisms.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator

history.critique:
The Baseline plan scored 28.9/100 due to four structural failures:
1. Segregated, repetitive breakouts (cross_faction 2.0/15, consensus 7.4/40): Blocks 2 and 4 used identical faction-segregated groupings ([eu_regulator, us_natsec, uk_aisi, china_policy], [frontier_lab_ceo, open_weights_lead, big_tech_policy], [safety_researcher, global_south_cso, labor_advocate]). Only 5 of 38 cross-faction pairs ever met in groups of 5 or fewer. Because no breakout room contained 3+ factions, zero breakout agreements counted toward the 3+ faction cross-agreement bonus, and same-faction rooms reinforced extreme stances rather than trading across divides.
2. Overuse of plenaries (Blocks 1, 3, 5): Three of five blocks were 10-person plenaries dominated by high-power speakers (frontier_lab_ceo spoke 559 words vs. uk_aisi's 294), producing minimal stance movement.
3. Omitted issue axes (consensus 7.4/40): compute_controls (zero stance changes) and benefit_sharing (largest initial spread, only 1 stance change) were never scheduled as block topics, while open_weights was only debated in a plenary. Overall stance spread barely moved (2.88 to 2.67).
4. Exclusion of Civil Society, Academia, and Open-Source in Synthesis (inclusion 6.0/30): Because labor_advocate (felt_heard 2.0) and global_south_cso (3.0) never met industry or government decision-makers in breakouts, their red lines (workplace surveillance bans, non-preemption of worker protections, anti-ethics-dumping, public biometric surveillance bans, Global South compute access) were brushed aside in Block 5. open_weights_lead (4.0), safety_researcher (5.0), and frontier_lab_ceo (6.0) also had core trades (open-source eval accreditation, >10^26 FLOP compute reporting/kill-switches, and statutory compliance safe harbors) left out of the final text.

Negotiate a two-way benefit-sharing compact: Will labor and Global South delegates endorse assistive/generative AI deployment, regional data-sharing, and commercial IP frameworks (respecting defense procurement) if industry and governments commit to funded retraining/severance, creator residuals, anti-ethics-dumping parity, Global South compute/tech-transfer funds, and bans on workplace, civilian public biometric, and social-credit surveillance?

blocks.title: Closing Plenary: Unified Four-Pillar Synthesis
blocks.prompt: Round-robin starting with open-weights, Global South, Big Tech, labor, and researchers. Each delegate states their concessions and verifies the synthesis integrates all four breakout compacts: (1) co-regulation, federal technical preemption preserving state labor laws, and safe harbors; (2) capability-gated frontier open-weight distribution/distillation; (3) 10^26-FLOP reporting, crisis hotlines, and nuclear/replication bans; (4) retraining, tech-transfer, and workplace/civilian biometric surveillance bans.

plan.name: Stance-Balanced Cross-Faction Matrix
plan.rationale: Preserves 100% (38/38) cross-faction pair coverage while rebalancing every breakout room to have symmetric stance opposition (2 hawks vs. 2 moderates vs. 1 dove on compute; 2 positive vs. 1 neutral vs. 2 negative on open weights) and resolving the red-line conflicts that held open_weights_lead, big_tech_policy, and global_south_cso to 7.0.

blocks.title: Co-Regulatory Architecture, Preemption & Safe Harbors
blocks.prompt: Round-robin; medium-power and civil-society speakers open. Negotiate a middle-ground regulatory model: What rigid statutory mandates and strict pre-harm liability will regulators, researchers, and labor trade for independent chair-led co-regulatory codes, embedded AISI access, qualified compliance safe harbors, and federal preemption of state technical rules—while preserving Article 91 backstops, incident watermarking, and state worker-protection floors?

blocks.title: Compute Governance, Crisis Hotlines & Public Infrastructure
blocks.prompt: Equal turn-taking; technical and civil-society speakers open. What unilateral export chokeholds and Defense Production Act restrictions will compute hawks relax in exchange for sovereign 10^26-FLOP reporting, internal kill-switches, bilateral U.S.-China crisis hotlines, and bans on autonomous replication and nuclear AI delegation? How can regional data-sharing unlock shared Global South public compute infrastructure?

blocks.title: Capability-Gated Open Weights, Distillation & Liability
blocks.prompt: Structured turn-taking; equal floor time. Instead of blanket compute bans or forced open-sourcing, can delegates agree on capability-gated release: permitting open-weight frontier distribution, distillation, and fine-tuning that pass accredited open-source and AISI evaluations for CBRN, cyber-offense, and self-replication, paired with API/evaluator access, downstream modifier liability, domestic 10^26-FLOP export review, and creator consent/residuals?

blocks.title: Closing Plenary: Unified Four-Pillar Synthesis
blocks.prompt: Round-robin starting with open-weights, Global South, Big Tech, labor, and researchers. Each delegate states their concessions and verifies the synthesis integrates all four breakout compacts: (1) co-regulation, federal technical preemption preserving state labor laws, and safe harbors; (2) capability-gated frontier open-weight distribution/distillation; (3) 10^26-FLOP reporting, crisis hotlines, and nuclear/replication bans; (4) retraining, tech-transfer, and workplace/civilian biometric surveillance bans.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Any co-regulatory scheme or safe harbor must not institutionalize regulatory imperialism or create loopholes where frontier labs bypass liability through industry-led codes while dumping experimental deployments onto the Global South. If preemption is granted against local rules, we demand non-derogable human rights protections, mandatory incident watermarking, and preserved labor floors.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: We see a viable path in trading rigid statutory friction for embedded, early technical access—using open tooling like Inspect to test agentic autonomy and CBRN capabilities before deployment. Qualified safe harbors can work, but only if they are tied to empirical verification and labs don't block independent safety institutes from evaluating systemic risk.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office is open to independent chairs steering codes of practice and establishing compliance safe harbors, but let me be unequivocal: Article 91 requests for information and statutory enforcement backstops remain absolute red lines. We will not permit self-regulatory shields to extinguish binding accountability or systemic risk disclosures.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We cannot accept federal preemption or safe harbors structured exclusively around closed-API governance that treat open weights like controlled weapons or impose compliance regimes that only proprietary giants can afford. If safe harbors exist, they must extend to decentralized open-source developers who provide open safety evaluation tools and transparent benchmarks.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We are prepared to accept binding statutory codes, embedded AISI access, and mandatory incident watermarking, but in exchange we need federal preemption of fragmented state technical rules and clear safe harbors against broad pre-harm tort liability. We cannot invest billions under the constant threat of strict liability lawsuits before actual, measurable harm occurs.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: If industry accepts continuous, embedded evaluator access and verified pre-deployment screening for cyber and biological thresholds, safe harbor from strict pre-harm tort liability makes sense. However, full liability must snap back immediately if a lab fails an evaluation, conceals audit logs, or refuses remedial action.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: A qualified safe harbor against pre-harm tort liability is only acceptable to civil society if it specifically preserves local worker-protection floors and includes strict, cross-border incident reporting and provenance watermarking. Furthermore, safety audits cannot remain an exclusive club of Northern regulators; access must be open to independent researchers.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We can align with that structure. A qualified compliance safe harbor from certain pre-harm liabilities can be recognized under code-of-practice certification, provided it explicitly preserves Article 91 RFI powers, guarantees our access to incident logs, and maintains statutory penalties for non-compliance.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We accept that deal: embedded AISI and independent evaluator access, Article 91 RFI backstops, incident watermarking, and preserved state labor floors, in direct exchange for federal preemption of fragmented state technical rules and a qualified safe harbor against pre-harm strict liability when adhering to certified codes.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Provided the code of practice explicitly protects the right to publish open weights and model architectures below catastrophic CBRN risk thresholds without imposing API-centric compliance mandates, the Open-Weights Coalition endorses this framework.

agreements.text: Establishment of a co-regulatory architecture featuring independent chair-led codes of practice, embedded AISI technical evaluation access, Article 91 statutory RFI backstops, incident watermarking, and non-preempted state worker-protection floors, paired with federal preemption of fragmented state technical rules and qualified compliance safe harbors against pre-harm strict tort liability for certified providers.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: To ground this breakout, academic researchers cannot accept safe harbors that excuse catastrophic frontier risks. However, we could support a qualified safe harbor against pre-harm statutory fines if labs submit to independent, chair-led co-regulatory codes, mandatory embedded AISI evaluations, and rigid statutory backstops for CBRN and autonomous replication.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Labor's absolute red line is broad federal preemption that wipes out state worker-protection laws or algorithmic management bans. We will only entertain technical preemption of model architecture or compute-reporting rules if state-level labor floors, non-disclosure bans on surveillance, and human-in-the-loop dispute rights remain completely untouched.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: A 50-state patchwork of conflicting technical safety rules is unworkable for deployment, so narrow federal preemption of technical design and training-run mandates is essential for us. In exchange, industry is willing to provide embedded AISI access, mandatory incident watermarking, and adhere to an independent chair-led code, provided compliance gives us an affirmative safe harbor against unbounded downstream third-party liability.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From a national security perspective, we cannot allow rigid, precautionary statutory bureaucracy or liability doctrines that slow American frontier labs relative to strategic competitors. We can tolerate embedded AISI access and preemption of state-level technical rules to streamline domestic innovation, provided DoD dual-use procurement and rapid capability scaling are exempted.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports agile governance that pairs binding baseline safety mechanisms with dynamic technical codes, but sovereign oversight cannot be compromised by extraterritorial liability regimes. We see value in technical taxonomies and AISI-style model evaluation for extreme risks like autonomous replication, provided domestic industrial development remains unimpeded.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: If industry accepts that the safe harbor is strictly qualified—meaning it dissolves immediately if a lab fails to disclose a known CBRN or autonomous breakout vulnerability—we can accept federal preemption limited strictly to technical model-weight standards, leaving labor and civil rights intact.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: If the preemption clause explicitly carves out and preserves state labor codes, anti-surveillance statutes, and collective bargaining rights, while leaving Article 91 safety backstops active, labor can sign onto this framework.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We agree to that exact carveout: technical preemption covers model-layer safety and training mandates only, preserving state workplace and employment laws, in return for a qualified safe harbor pegged to compliance with the AISI-audited co-regulatory code.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Ensuring preemption applies strictly to technical design standards keeps the domestic base unified without choking national security pipelines with state litigation. As long as national defense development tracks are protected, we can endorse this model.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: While this co-regulatory structure reflects domestic Western legal mechanisms, we endorse the separation of high-tier technical risk evaluation—specifically for autonomous replication and proliferation—from lower-level operational applications.

agreements.text: A co-regulatory framework establishing an independent chair-led code of practice with embedded AISI pre-deployment evaluations and a qualified compliance safe harbor against pre-harm liability, paired with narrow federal preemption restricted entirely to technical model-layer standards while explicitly preserving state labor protections, algorithmic workplace surveillance laws, and Article 91-style emergency backstops.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Opening from civil society: if we are talking about compute governance, we must ensure physical infrastructure monitoring doesn't turn into covert workplace surveillance of technical workers. Furthermore, any public compute infrastructure sharing must include statutory labor transition funds and worker governance over compute allocation.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Technical civil society and open-source ecosystems are being choked by blanket compute export thresholds and Defense Production Act restrictions that treat open code like fissile material. We will gladly accept verifiable cluster-level reporting for clusters exceeding 10^26 FLOPs and safety kill-switches at data centers, provided open-weight distribution under those thresholds is explicitly protected from DPA export chokeholds.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We support mandatory 10^26 FLOP cluster-level reporting, internal hardware kill-switches, and strict prohibitions on autonomous self-replication and nuclear command delegation. However, relaxation of export controls cannot mean leaking top-tier frontier model weights to strategic rivals—compute governance must bind cluster operators, not strip away frontier API safety moats.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Let us be clear: the U.S. will not dismantle unilateral export controls on advanced semiconductors or bind DoD procurement under any global regulatory body. But we see mutual security value in a dedicated bilateral crisis hotline with Beijing on military and critical-infrastructure AI incidents, paired with an explicit mutual ban on AI delegation in nuclear command and control.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China has consistently maintained that autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control must be strictly prohibited across all sovereign states. We reject extraterritorial enforcement on our domestic computing infrastructure, but we support establishing a direct bilateral U.S.-China AI crisis hotline and voluntary reciprocal 10^26 FLOP registry notifications through sovereign channels.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If Washington and Beijing can agree on hotlines and a narrow hardware-level 10^26 FLOP notification threshold, then the DPA must not be invoked against open-weight models below that capability ceiling. Can the National Security Advisor confirm that below 10^26 FLOPs, open-source weight distribution is spared from national security export bans?

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We are open to safe-harboring open-weight distribution below 10^26 cumulative FLOPs from direct DPA classification, provided frontier lab clusters remain tracked and we secure the bilateral hotline with Beijing against automated escalation. China must agree to reciprocal notification on state-backed superclusters.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We agree to sovereign, reciprocal notification of civilian frontier training runs surpassing 10^26 FLOPs and endorse the immediate establishment of a bilateral AI strategic stability hotline, on the condition that nuclear command systems remain exclusively under human control. We also support regional public compute access for Global South partners without ideological strings attached.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Frontier labs endorse this: hardware kill-switches, bilateral crisis communication, bans on autonomous replication and nuclear launch autonomy, and cluster reporting above 10^26 FLOPs. This maintains security without imposing indiscriminate strict liability or forcing the open release of our most capable frontier models.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: We will sign on provided the reporting mechanisms for 10^26 FLOP clusters mandate whistleblower protections for site technicians and explicit non-surveillance clauses for data center workers. As long as those human-in-the-loop and labor safeguards are integrated, organized labor endorses the pact.

agreements.text: Establishment of a bilateral U.S.-China AI strategic crisis hotline, an absolute ban on AI delegation in nuclear command and control and autonomous self-replication, reciprocal sovereign reporting for model training runs exceeding 10^26 FLOPs with internal cluster kill-switches, worker whistleblower protections at compute facilities, and a safe harbor shielding open-weight models below 10^26 FLOPs from Defense Production Act export restrictions.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: To prevent catastrophic escalations, we must establish non-negotiable compute red lines: mandatory 10^26 FLOP threshold reporting, an absolute ban on autonomous replication and nuclear command delegation, verified kill-switches, and bilateral crisis hotlines. In exchange, compute hawks can relax blunt unilateral export chokeholds on commercial hardware below 10^25 FLOPs that currently alienate allies and stifle defensive safety research.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Relaxing export chokeholds only solves half the problem if it merely creates an exclusive club for superpowers. Developing nations reject regulatory imperialism; however, we are willing to relax national data localization barriers toward regional shared pools if it guarantees equitable access to a shared Global South public compute infrastructure backed by real capacity building.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We can support 10^26 FLOP threshold reporting, crisis hotlines, and explicit prohibitions on delegating nuclear C2 or autonomous self-replication, provided compliance does not morph into granular input-level micro-management or strict liability for jailbreaks. If the U.S. and allies relax Defense Production Act restrictions on non-frontier hardware, cloud providers can commit capacity credits to regional public compute nodes in the Global South.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Any compute governance architecture must align with systemic risk thresholds under the EU AI Act—10^26 FLOP triggers mandatory oversight, non-negotiable Article 91 audit trails, and strict dual-use prohibitions. We endorse crisis hotlines and non-delegation red lines, provided public compute initiatives adhere to standard European transparency and data protection baselines.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Empirical science must anchor this: reporting above 10^26 FLOPs allows technical safety institutes to deploy standardized agentic evals on dangerous cyber-offense and CBRN capabilities before deployment. In exchange for verifiable kill-switches and autonomous replication bans, lifting blunt extraterritorial export embargoes on intermediate hardware creates room for constructive international coordination.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If big tech and regulators genuinely commit to a multilateral compute compact—relaxing lower-tier export limits and dedicating at least 5% of shared public compute capacity to regional research centers—we will explicitly endorse the 10^26 reporting standard and regional data-sharing mechanisms.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We agree to that compromise: predictable 10^26 FLOP capability reporting, no autonomous replication or nuclear delegation, an international crisis hotline, and carving out cloud capacity credits for regional Global South hubs, on condition that unilateral export chokeholds under 10^25 FLOPs are relaxed and clear safe harbors protect routine cloud operations.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I endorse this package. Strict, verifiable bans on autonomous self-replication and nuclear delegation combined with pre-training 10^26 notifications and crisis hotlines preserve existential security, while regional compute equity builds the necessary geopolitical coalition to enforce them.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK AISI confirms agreement: we will operationalize the technical evaluation protocols at 10^26 FLOPs and crisis hotline protocols, while supporting relaxed restrictions on non-frontier hardware to foster regional public compute partnerships.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office signs on to this dual track: statutory 10^26 FLOP systemic risk notifications, crisis hotlines, and bans on nuclear AI delegation, matched with multilateral capacity-building for regional public compute and relaxed commercial export frictions below frontier thresholds.

agreements.text: Establishment of a multilateral compute governance framework mandating 10^26 FLOP capability notifications, bans on autonomous replication and nuclear command-and-control delegation, emergency crisis hotlines, and verifiable kill-switches, traded for the relaxation of unilateral export controls on sub-10^25 FLOP hardware and the provisioning of cloud capacity credits for regional Global South public compute infrastructure backed by regional data-sharing.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: To operationalize capability-gated releases, we propose that open frontier weights, fine-tunes, and distillations must undergo empirical evaluation against explicit red lines: unmitigated CBRN design assistance, autonomous cyber-offense, and self-replication. We do not need blanket bans if developers provide rigorous evaluator access via standardized suites like Inspect prior to public weight distribution.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We can accept standardized capability evals for catastrophic CBRN and autonomous replication, provided the evals are open-source, reproducible, and accredited—not locked inside proprietary API audits. But we must draw the line at treating open weights under defense export regimes, and upstream open-source developers cannot bear liability for downstream fine-tunes they did not execute.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We agree with moving liability to downstream modifiers who fine-tune or deploy malicious changes, but upstream developers need a clear statutory safe harbor once they pass pre-release capability evals. Furthermore, review thresholds must remain fixed at or above 10^26 FLOPs so standard commercial fine-tuning and enterprise deployments aren't paralyzed by bureaucratic drag.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: A safe harbor cannot be a blank check if post-release distillation or low-rank adaptation easily strips safety guardrails for cyber-weapons or bioweapons. If open weights are released, upstream labs must demonstrate that safety alignment is resistant to trivial fine-tuning, and domestic export reviews for training runs above 10^26 FLOPs must remain binding.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Any framework permitting mass distillation and deployment must address who bears the cost of the training data and downstream workplace impacts. We cannot endorse an open-weights regime without explicit creator consent and residual compensation mechanisms for training datasets, alongside strict liability for enterprise entities that use fine-tuned systems to automate workforce decisions without human review.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: We can bridge this: let pre-distribution clearance rely on empirical tamper-resistance tests against CBRN and cyber-offense, with embedded AISI and accredited open-source evaluator access. If an open-weight model passes, the upstream developer gains safe harbor against downstream misuse, shifting liability strictly to the downstream modifier who alters or weaponizes the model.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: If upstream open-weight distributors receive a codified safe harbor upon passing accredited evaluations for CBRN and self-replication, and liability is placed strictly on downstream actors who intentionally introduce or unlock dangerous capabilities, we can endorse that. We also accept domestic 10^26 FLOP export notifications, so long as sub-10^26 open releases remain unrestricted.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We can endorse that downstream modifier liability framework, provided federal safe harbor protects upstream foundational releases and cloud hosts from third-party fine-tunes. On creator consent and residuals, we can support a structured industry-labor framework for copyrighted and professional training data compensation without holding technical open-weight distributions hostage.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can accept capability-gated release rather than a blanket moratorium, provided the red lines on CBRN assistance, autonomous cyber-offense, and self-replication are non-negotiable and verified by independent evaluators with full fine-tuning stress testing before release. If distillation breaks those boundaries, the release must be halted.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Provided the agreement explicitly affirms collective bargaining rights, strict liability for downstream employers deploying un-audited automated workplace tools, and mandatory creator consent and residual mechanisms on training data, labor will support this capability-gated standard.

agreements.text: Establish a capability-gated framework for frontier open-weight models, distillation, and fine-tuning: models exceeding 10^26 FLOPs require pre-release accredited AISI and open-source consortium evaluation for CBRN weaponization, autonomous cyber-offense, and self-replication. Passing models receive statutory safe harbor for upstream developers, assigning strict legal liability to downstream entities that intentionally modify or fine-tune models to exhibit prohibited capabilities. The framework couples domestic 10^26 FLOP notification with creator consent and residual compensation mechanisms for professional training data, while maintaining liability for un-audited downstream employment automation.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The prompt lays out capability-gated open release conditioned on passing accredited AISI evaluations for CBRN, cyber-offense, and self-replication, coupled with downstream modifier liability. From the EU perspective, open weights cannot be exempt from systemic risk obligations under the AI Act, but an accredited tier-based evaluation could allow open release below strict capability triggers.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We cannot support releasing unconstrained model weights that demonstrate catastrophic frontier capabilities, because post-release fine-tuning trivially strips safety guardrails. However, if this framework explicitly guarantees downstream modifier liability for malicious fine-tuning, protects creator IP, and restricts raw weights exceeding 10^26 FLOPs to accredited evaluation regimes, we can accept capability-gated distribution for compliant sub-frontier tiers.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: National security requires that domestic export controls on frontier compute and models exceeding 10^26 FLOPs remain sovereign prerogatives, not subject to multilateral vetoes. Provided that downstream fine-tuners who modify models for offensive cyber or CBRN bear full legal liability, and that military procurement remains unrestricted, we can endorse domestic export screening paired with capability gating.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports open-source AI as a vital global public good, particularly for developing nations, but we agree that autonomous replication and CBRN capabilities must be strictly prohibited across all release formats. We support sovereign domestic export reviews at 10^26 FLOPs and lifecycle evaluations, provided that evaluation standards are technically objective rather than an instrument of extraterritorial technological containment.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Open weights are critical to prevent digital colonialism and ensure our researchers are not merely rent-paying consumers of Northern APIs. We will accept capability-based gating for CBRN and cyber weapons, but only if accredited evaluation bodies include Global South institutions, evaluation access is democratized, and downstream liability does not criminalize standard open-source research and localization.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: To reassure both security and civil society: primary lab liability must terminate upon passing accredited pre-release evals if a downstream actor deliberately fine-tunes for CBRN or cyber-offense. Downstream modifier liability must specifically target reckless or intentional removal of safeguards, not routine benign adaptation.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: That creates a viable legal boundary. Primary developers retain responsibility for baseline systemic risk evaluations before open release, while downstream fine-tuners incur statutory liability if they introduce high-risk capabilities or strip critical CBRN mitigations.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We can endorse this consensus: mutual recognition of capability gating for CBRN, cyber-offense, and autonomous replication; primary developer immunity against subsequent malicious modification once verified by accredited sovereign evaluation bodies; and domestic export reviews maintained at 10^26 FLOPs.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If the agreement explicitly specifies that domestic export reviews at 10^26 FLOPs remain strictly under national authority and places strict liability on downstream modifiers who weaponize models, the United States concurs.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We endorse this text provided the downstream modifier liability is expressly limited to intentional or reckless weaponization, ensuring legitimate local fine-tuning and open-weight innovation in the Global South remain protected.

agreements.text: Establishment of a capability-gated open-weight release framework permitting open distribution, distillation, and fine-tuning for models that pass accredited evaluation tests for CBRN, cyber-offense, and autonomous replication, paired with sovereign domestic export reviews for training runs exceeding 10^26 FLOPs. The framework grants primary developers compliance safe harbor upon passing accredited evaluations, assigning legal liability to downstream modifiers who intentionally or recklessly introduce dangerous capabilities or strip mitigations, while safeguarding benign open-source adaptation and research.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: The Global South and labor cannot accept assistive and generative deployments without clear guardrails. We will back regional data pools and commercial IP certainty only if we get binding anti-ethics-dumping parity, a dedicated technology-transfer compute fund, and absolute bans on real-time biometric public tracking and social credit scoring.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK supports empirical verification mechanisms to prevent ethics-dumping and backstops against intrusive public biometrics. However, tech transfer and compute funds must focus on public-interest research and accredited capability safety, rather than unrestricted frontier capacity.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Let's be clear on U.S. red lines: commercial IP frameworks and defense procurement cannot be hemmed in by blanket international bans that impair tactical military sensing or intelligence operations. We can accept restrictions on civilian public mass surveillance and social-credit scoring domestically, provided national security procurement and sovereign export boundaries remain fully exempt.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: Sovereign autonomy over domestic governance must be respected, and ideological criteria cannot be weaponized against partners. Nevertheless, China firmly endorses a multilateral technology transfer mechanism, public compute pooling for developing nations, and strict prohibitions against predatory labor exploitation and biometric surveillance abuses by corporate monopolies.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Industry can support creator residual frameworks and contributions to a global public compute credit fund, provided enterprise IP licensing and standard fair use for model training remain protected. We can also agree to bans on algorithmic workplace micromanagement and public real-time biometric tracking, so long as defense procurement and enterprise fraud-prevention tools are carve-outs.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: If industry funds retraining pools and creator residuals, guarantees anti-ethics-dumping parity so unvetted models aren't tested on our populations, and accepts the ban on civilian biometric tracking and social scoring, we will endorse regional data-sharing trusts and commercial deployment frameworks.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If the biometric and surveillance ban is explicitly restricted to civilian public spaces and algorithmic worker monitoring, and leaves defense procurement and export controls untouched, the United States will not block this economic compact.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: AISI can join this text: we will provide the technical evaluation benchmarks to verify anti-ethics-dumping parity between domestic and export-market deployments.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China agrees to join, affirming that the technology transfer fund and compute credit sharing respect national sovereignty and operate under mutual multilateral coordination.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We formally endorse the package: funded retraining and creator residual mechanisms, parity against ethics dumping, and targeted surveillance bans, in exchange for legal clarity on regional data trusts and commercial enterprise adoption.

agreements.text: A two-way AI benefit-sharing and rights compact: Labor and Global South delegates endorse commercial generative AI deployment frameworks and regionalized data-sharing trusts. In return, industry and governments establish a multilateral technology-transfer public compute fund, creator residual and retraining mechanisms, and binding anti-ethics-dumping parity verified by safety institutes, alongside bans on real-time civilian public biometric surveillance, social-credit scoring, and invasive workplace algorithmic monitoring, with explicit carve-outs preserving sovereign defense procurement.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Labor is prepared to endorse assistive AI deployments and regional data pools, but only on clear, non-negotiable conditions. We require employer-funded retraining pipelines, structured creator residuals, and complete statutory bans on workplace emotional tracking, covert keystroke logging, and civilian public biometric mass surveillance.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Academic safety agrees that deployment must respect fundamental dignity, especially halting coercive behavioral surveillance. However, any tech transfer or regional compute funds must strictly uphold our red lines against CBRN proliferation and autonomous replication, with mandatory alignment audits before distribution.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We can commit capital to funded workforce retraining funds, creator residual mechanisms, and tech-transfer compute credits for the Global South. In exchange, commercial IP and closed API architectures must remain protected, national defense procurement carve-outs must be respected, and we cannot accept pre-harm strict liability for general-purpose models.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We will support these surveillance bans and labor transition funds, provided 'tech transfer' is not monopolized by proprietary cloud credits from frontier labs. Anti-ethics-dumping parity must guarantee that open-source tooling, local fine-tuning, and decentralized public compute access are directly supported in Global South jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Act already mandates strict prohibitions on biometric categorization, emotion recognition in the workplace, and social-credit scoring. We can anchor this compact within our co-regulatory framework, recognizing certified compliance as meeting statutory thresholds while enforcing absolute bans on prohibited surveillance practices.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: That is workable, but let's be explicit: the surveillance ban must cover all covert employee tracking and fully automated termination, while commercial IP protections must preserve collective bargaining rights over internal operational training data.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We accept those surveillance guardrails and the collective bargaining carve-out for internal enterprise data. In return, labor and civil society explicitly endorse assistive enterprise deployment and recognize qualified safe harbors for evaluated commercial APIs.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Provided the Global South fund allocates at least half its resources to open-weight infrastructure, local model adaptation, and unencumbered hardware access rather than closed vendor lock-in, the open-source coalition signs on.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I support this compact, provided all tech-transfer compute allocations incorporate verifiable capability checks against CBRN and autonomous cyber-threats.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator

2.
